# Executive summary 

<mark>The change in sentiment since the last LTO, against a backdrop of an even weaker economic outlook in conjunction with a waning interest from commodity investors, has led us to temper our price forecasts this year and over the medium term.  Our global market surplus is little changed for this year as a consequence of the revisions made to both production and consumption estimates for 2012.  The deficit now stands at ~130kt with stocks at 48 days of consumption for the year.  However, we have lowered our average price forecast to $7937/t ($3.60/lb) from $8580/t ($3.89/lb) in 2011$.  This decline reflects a much weaker than anticipated price environment for the year thus far.  The main impetus remains the ongoing uncertainty as a result of the resurgence of the Euro crisis initially in Greece, but now spreading to Spain and possibly Italy.  Prices have been swept lower by the deteriorating economic news and further dampened by an ongoing</mark> appreciation in the US dollar. 

<mark>The net result of our changes to consumption has been to lower year-on-year global demand growth in 2011 to 2.4% from 2.7% in the Q1 2012 LTO report as more complete annual data comes through.  This mainly reflects the softer tone across Oceania, South Korea and Taiwan.  In 2012, global growth has been downgraded to 2.7% from 3.7% as economic woes continue to impact consumer off-take of cathode.  Meanwhile disruptions remain a factor in the supply chain, with inclement weather and slower than planned ramp up at several mines the key contributors to our weaker production estimates of 20.205Mt this year.  We remain committed to our view of higher prices in the second half of this year, supported by the anticipated recovery in China.  The inventories that have built up over Q4 2011 and into this year are expected to be whittled steadily lower as the Chinese economy rebounds.  This should also provide some upward momentum to prices to average $8300/t by Q4 2012 as stocks days to consumption slip back to 48 days against a backdrop of a persistent deficit over the latter half of this year.</mark> 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 0.6% p.a. between 2011 and 2025 due to resource depletion with output falling from just under 21Mt in 2015 to slightly less than 15Mt in 2025.  In 2011, demand for mine production exceeded available base case supply by c.430kt, higher than our Q1 estimate of a

round 300kt but within the range of analysis over the course of this year.  We expect the market to move closer to balance this year of c.120kt, while metal from projects under construction will likely push the market into surplus in 2013 and 2014.  From 2015 onwards, demand for mine output should once again exceed available base case supply.  This shortfall will be satisfied either by the reactivation of closed mines, new ore discoveries at currently producing mines, incremental expansions, mine life extensions or the development of greenfield projects. 

Our smelter production capability forecast for 2012 is 16.5Mt, representing a 6.8% increase from 2011, although a lack of concentrates and scrap is likely to moderate this increase to just 2.4% in terms of actual production.  Smelter output capability growth is expected to remain strong over the next two years at 8.9% in 2013 and 6.6% in 2014, primarily as a result of increased mine feed although increasing smelter capacity in China and India should also contribute.  A total of 4.8Mt of additional smelter production capability is expected over the forecast period with just over half coming from China. 

The majority of the revisions made to our smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in the changes to our refinery output estimates and these can be seen in the main report.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production rose by 3.6% to 19.7Mt/a in 2011, while capability is expected to increase by a substantial 9.6% this year, to 21.6Mt.  A further 9% year-on-year increment in 2013 will see this figure rise to 23.5Mt/a in 2013, and then to 24.8Mt in 2014.  However, growth is forecast to slow markedly in 2015, and then to decline from 2016 onwards. As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.4% p.a. between 2010 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~4.37Mt to 23.38Mt in 2025. 

<mark>Our profile of a market moving into surplus from 2013 remains in place and as mine output begins to come through to market from the slew of projects that are starting to ramp up we expect to see surpluses of ~500kt over the three year period 2013 to 2015.  Despite the emergence of this additional material, metal stock days to consumption of 54 days are still below average and prices in 2013 should remain above $3.00/lb on average in 2011$.  As production plays catch up and we enter a period of high mine growth, prices will yield to the persistent build in inventories (to average 66 days of consumption) and trend below $3.00/lb in 2011$ from 2015 to 2018.  The risk remains that weaker copper prices and a tougher financial climate could derail some of the copper projects that are due to come on stream over the medium to long term.  We feel there is less downside risk to our consumption forecast unless there are any significant new</mark> developments in the Eurozone debt crisis situation which would likely have considerable impact

on demand globally. Beyond 2018 and through to 2025 we expect prices to average at our project incentive price of $6614/t ($3.00/lb) in constant 2011$. These forecasts remain well above the 90th percentile of C1 cash costs on a Composite Costing basis. Historically, marginal costs have been a good proxy for determining where annual average copper prices will decline to, but only during periods of excessive metal inventories. However, our analysis points to only moderate metal surpluses occurring at certain stages over the forecast period, reflecting a market that continues to struggle to keep up with consumption and maintain stocks at the average 65 days of consumption over the medium to long term. This compares to 3.7% in our previously forecast. We have trimmed our expectations of Chinese refined consumption growth in 2012 to 7% from 8% and also downgraded our views on South Korea and Taiwan from neutral to outright declines this year based on disappointing year-to-date trends and lower semis exports to China. 2012 full year prospects in Italy, France and Germany have also been cut based on a poor H1 performance. However, we have raised our forecasts for Sweden, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia which provides some offset to the downward revisions elsewhere. North American demand has exceeded expectations so far and it is also more likely that we would also be revising up our South American full year consumption numbers if the momentum from a strong Q1 is carried forward into Q2. Brazil - as the largest consuming market - is at the heart of the recovery, but there is also a strong collective contribution from all the other countries within the continent. ## China 

**Sluggish first half tempers 2011** The disappointing start to the year for Chinese demand continued through the second quarter to leave question marks hanging over the full year forecast.  We were always of the opinion that consumption would be strongest in the second half of this year as the economy picks up pace again after the controlled slowdown that has been engineered by authorities.  Since the last _Long Term Outlook_ there have been a series of measures introduced to boost economic activity, including white goods incentive schemes and infrastructure investment, not to mention a cut in interest rates.  This should combine to boost consumption in the second half of the year given that many of the measures introduced are likely to directly impact on demand for copper.  Even though we are confident of a H2 recovery, the weakness of the first half has led us to downgrade our expectations for growth in 2012 to 7% from 8% previously, although we have lifted our forecast for 2013 to 7.5%.  Between 2011 to 2016, copper demand growth is expected to average c. 7% per year, before slowing to 4.8% through the remainder of the forecast period. 

**Downstream trade paints the backdrop to Chinese growth story** The charts below illustrate some of the longer term trends taking place in the Chinese market.  Exports of copper products have grown rapidly over the past ten years, although the trend was briefly interrupted by a collapse in 2009 during the financial crisis.  Through the same period, China has gradually reduced its reliance on imports of those same products as the country massively increased its downstream semis capacity in a bid to create an integrated economy and to produce higher value products.  Over the same time period, China’s apparent consumption of copper increased sharply as it produced more semis and wire and cable that it previously imported while China also recently became a net exporter of copper products.  Depending on one’s mindset this could be interpreted in different ways but crucially, this does point to China’s reliance on the health of world export markets in order to contribute to its future growth.  That does raise some concerns over very near term growth prospects, although given the relatively consistent trajectory of both imports and exports, this would suggest that Chinese demand will continue to grow over the medium term.  This will be because of a lesser requirement for semis imports as these are met by domestic production but also as a result of increased demand for Chinese exports from overseas countries.  Indeed, our long term forecasts point to declining first use consumption of copper in key developed regions around the world, including North America, Western Eu

rope and Japan. It is important to remember that just because a country is reducing their first use consumption of refined copper, it does not necessarily mean they are consuming less copper in product form or indeed, through the consumption of copper containing end use products. **Total net trade of copper products by Cu content – (kt)** **Mixed signals from downstream capacity investment** The near term weakness in Chinese copper demand and semis production is underscored by Jiangxi Copper’s announcement at the end of May that it is to delay the start up of its new 400kt/a rod mill in Guangdong province, which is set to be the world’s largest when it goes into production. This is to be deferred into the second half of the year, so not a massive delay but it does highlight the cautious tone to current demand though it also confirms our own view of improvements to come in the second half. Elsewhere, Wuxi Lineo, a rod and cable company in Jiangsu, is investing in a new 120kt/a rod line in Bengbu city, Anhui province in an expansion away from its home province. The name of the new company is Anhu Lineo Copper industry and will use Chinese Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - June 2012 Page 6 of 39 Copper Long Term Outlook continuous casting technology for the line which is due to be commissioned later this year. However, set against these second half expansions, Jiangxi Dahua Copper has already started production at its 100kt/a rod line, in Yingtan City, Jianxi Province, while Eastern Copper 320kt/a wire rod project in Shandong province also began operating in May, although this SMS Meer continuous caster is set to use scrap as its main feed source. Finally, Zhejiang Honglei’s new 150kt/a wire rod line st

arted trial production in May, with output said to be mainly focussed on serving internal magnet wire production. Turning towards brass mills, Golden dragon, the largest copper tube producer in China, has invested 380m RMB to build a 30kt/a ACR tube mill in Luoyang city, Henan province. Construction started recently and the tube mill is expected to be commissioned in 2013/2014. Ningbo Powerway, a copper and alloy rod producer in China, is building a sheet/strip line with capacity of 40ktpa, which will be commissioned this year. **Infrastructure boost to lift electrical sector** The key sector to underpin demand growth for this year was always going to be the electrical sector and recent announcements on infrastructure projects have been reassuring against the backdrop of a relatively sluggish start to the year overall. The government is to bring forward investment on a range of infrastructure investments but importantly part of this will be on energy. Previous comments from the State Council had suggested infrastructure investment would likely grow by 15-20% this year, with the latest announcement set to lift this further, although this does not mean a direct read across to sectoral copper demand. Indeed, part of the growth in power investment has benefited aluminium overhead power cable and bare conductors as investment in the inner and western provinces has been installed aerially rather than underground. Even so, we still remain relatively bullish on demand prospects later this year and further out. Indeed, as the chart below reveals, initial plans for investment tend to be much lower than the final outcome, while plans for investment are also upgraded over time. **Motor vehicle production to support growth through medium term** Another sector that is expected to support demand for copper both this year and through the medium term is automotive, with car production in particular set to bounce back this year after a sluggish 2011. In fact, we forecast car output will increase by c.8% this year and at an average rate of 7-8% in the period 2011 to 2016, before moderating thereafter to average c.3% through the remainder of the forecast period. Crucially, increases in the average copper content of cars as a result of the “average” vehicle becoming more sophisticated and including more gadgets will propel demand for copper at a rate in excess of vehicle production growth. Meanwhile, the increasing pe

netration of hybrid and electric vehicles, which are also more copper intensive, will support the growth trajectory of copper demand ahead of vehicle production.  China is also a major assembler of wiring harness for export. 

**Construction growth to moderate from breakneck pace** The sharp pace of growth that the Chinese construction market has experienced over the past few years is set to ease both this year and through the longer term according to our analysis.  The slowdown this year is easily explained by the sharp focus that the sector is under as authorities clamp down on speculation in the real estate market in order to tame prices and prevent a property bubble.  The lag between starts and copper use should support demand through this year, although admittedly at a lower pace than has been seen recently, although prospects for 2013 look less certain.  Over the longer term, a number of factors will combine to limit growth in new building, not least that so much has already taken place.  For example, the standard of construction work and materials have improved dramatically over the past few years and a building that lasts longer does not need to be replaced as often and thus slowing the rate of new construction activity.  Although we forecast continued growth in construction activity in the western and central provinces, this is likely to be offset by much more sluggish activity on the

**Consumer products to benefit from incentives in short term** After an extremely sluggish start to the year for demand for consumer goods, the government has intervened to boost purchases.  Indeed, the State Council has announced a 26.5 billion yuan ($4.2 billion) scheme to subsidise the purchase of energy saving household electrical appliances for a one-year period.  Goods covered include air conditioners, flat-panel television sets, refrigerators, washing machines and water heaters that meet energy-saving standards.  However, it is important to note that this scheme is much smaller than those announced in the aftermath of the financial crisis and its impact is to be more muted.  Moreover, we understand that there are significant stocks of consumer products in the supply chain and as a result, these will have to be worked off before production can begin to pick up.  The downside to these schemes, however, is that they tend to bring forward purchases and as such, they are possibly reducing demand in the following years, although China Inc. will be hoping that overseas markets will be staging a recovery by then.  The medium term outlook for the consumer sector remains firm, although towards the latter part of our forecast period Chinese goods will likely become less compet

However, as we have moved through the year, reported data has told a slightly different story. Looking at the first quarter alone, wire rod production was up by 2.5% to 332.8kt, however, data for the first four months of the year reveals that output is actually down by 0.4%, after a slump in April. At the same time, apparent consumption data also points to a modest contraction in demand. Our view is that overall consumption was up in the first quarter but only by a little but this is broadly in line with our forecast for the full year, with demand expected to climb by 1.1% to 1839kt in 2012. North America as a whole is expected to grow at a similar rate this year and for the period 2011 to 2016 we expect demand growth to average 1.7%, with an acceleration through 2013 to 2015 supporting this average rate. Beyond 2016, however, we foresee a contraction in first use demand as downstream facilities face negative cost headwinds which will result in declining semis production and an average annual decline of almost 2%. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - June 2012 Page 8 of 39 Copper Long Term Outlook **Downstream investment to temper long term decline?** Despite the gloomy long term prognosis outlined above, there have been some recent investments in downstream capacity in the US, with SDI-LaFarga’s, new rod mill in Indiana commissioned during June, Golden Dragon’s Alabama based tube plant set for 2013 production, while Nexans have broken ground at their extra high voltage facility in South Carolina. The SDI-LaFarga joint venture is interesting because it will be fed entirely from No.2 scrap rather than cathode and reportedly began test production at the 80-90kt/a line in mid-June. Given that the plant is unlikely to meet or create new demand for rod, the prognosis is therefore

that it will take market share from existing players and Canadian and Mexican imports and in doing so temper demand for cathode. In the meantime, the plant has been stocking up on scrap and this has tightened the domestic scrap market and in doing so, somewhat ironically, this has resulted in other semis producers switching from scrap to cathode because of the scarcity of scrap. The extent to which scrap consumption at the plant reduces scrap exports or tightens domestic discounts remains to be seen, as does the full impact that this will have on cathode consumption in the short and medium term. Other investments that have caught our attention are Henan, China-based Golden Dragon Precise Copper Tube Inc., increasing the size of its planned new investment in Alabama. It will now build a US$100M plant at Pine Hill, Wilcox County in Alabama, using cast and roll tube-making technology, and this should allow the company to avoid getting hit by anti-competitive trade legislation which has affected its imports into the US from its plants in China and Mexico. Plant capacity and start-up time have yet to be released, though we would expect no less than 30-50kt/a, given the economics of such a unit and the company’s existing presence in the sector. The plant is likely to go into production some time in 2013. One final piece of investment news is Nexans’ announcement that it has broken ground at its extra high voltage cable facility in South Carolina. The facility is to produce underground cables of 500 kV following this US$85m investment and is set to begin production in 2014, although this will be at relatively small volumes. Taken together, these announcements suggest a brighter outlook for the American copper market, although we are less upbeat about the longer term prospects for demand. Firstly, as we noted above, the SDI-LaFarga mill will be fed by scrap and this will do nothing to directly support refined copper demand. Meanwhile, the investment from Nexans is positive but this will increase demand for wire rod and this could well be met by imports and as such, will not necessarily support domestic demand for cathode. As we noted above, we remain of the opinion that following a few years of growth, the North American refined copper will shift into contraction mode as semis production shifts to lower cost locations. ##### **US copper wire rod production - (kt)** 20 500

**Building on firm foundations** The construction sector has been quietly recovering since the second half of last year, with housing starts on a solid upward trajectory since then but because of the lag between starting

to build a house and copper consumption, the improvement was not initially felt by semis producers.  However, this has now started to change, with producers reporting renewed interest from the sector, which should continue to build momentum given our growth forecasts over the next few years.  Total construction spend in the US contracted every single year between 2006 and 2011, although 2012 is set to break this losing streak, with investment forecast to expand by 4.5% in total, with residential investment driving this strength.  Total construction investment is then set to grow by 5-6% per year out to 2016, before easing back thereafter.  The bad news, however, is that there is not a direct read across to copper demand growth from the sector.  This is because anecdotally we are hearing that average homes are getting smaller and this is tempering the upswing, although it is unclear whether this will become a consistent future trend.  If it did, this could put sectoral demand on a permanently lower trajectory.  Meanwhile, some of the recent growth has been buoyed by increased investment in multi-family units, ie apartments, which would also have a lower copper intensity rather than a house, which has also served to reduce the overall average copper intensity of construction.

**Autos hit top gear** The strength of the automotive market has been the saving grace of the US economy over the past few years, with car output growing by 8.6% last year even in the face of disruptions to supply chains from the Japanese earthquake.  This year looks to be even better, with production expected to expand by just under 17%.  It is also forecast to record double-digit growth in 2013 before slowing sharply by 2015.  After three years of sharp contractions in output between 2007 and 2009 there was a large amount of pent up demand for new vehicles and this is now resulting in improved car sales, while easier access to credit is also lending a hand.  In line with the production outlook, we forecast firm growth in sectoral demand for copper this year and through to 2014 before slowing sharply thereafter.

Q1 had begun reasonably well, especially in Scandinavia and the United Kingdom, but German wire rod mills were already detecting a soft start in their export sales to the major consuming markets of France, Spain and Italy. The uncertainties posed by the possibility of a Greek default and an exit from the Euro, coupled with instability in the banking sector in Spain and Italy, have combined to effectively drain any momentum from the market through the second quarter. With little short term improvement expected or warranted we would expect to see lengthy late summer holiday / maintenance mill shutdowns in southern Europe this year. Consumers will await clearer economic news and sentiment and gauge order interest come September. **Telecom cablemakers enter administration** Within the wire and cable industry there is a wide variation in performance by product line. The small copper telecom cable market faces an uncertain future with both the United Kingdom producer B3 (Blackley, Manchester) and its Spanish subsidiary B3 Solutions Spain (Santander) both entering administration in early June due to “difficult trading conditions”. However, B3’s other UK subsidiary Tri-Wire, which manufactures bare and tinned copper wire from its site in Normanton has found new buyers in the form of Anglia Metal safeguarding 31 jobs. **EHV / HV powers on** The situation in the high voltage power cable segment could not be more different. Prysmian has just invested €40 million to open a new submarine power cable plant in Pikkala, Finland, which was inaugurated in earlyJune. This move expands Prysmian’s capacity

at this location and adds High Voltage Direct Current technology to its portfolio.  Prysmian is also in the process of expanding its Arco Felice submarine power cable plant near Naples in Italy. These sites, together with its Drammen facility in Norway, will fulfil the €800 million Western Link project to construct and lay a submarine power cable link between Scotland and England.  Orders for power distribution cables were again stronger in northern Europe than in the south with the exception of Scandinavia and France (the latter mainly favours

**ASEAN consumption prospects burn brightest** The Indian refined copper consumption outlook is currently readjusting to a phase of much slower progress. Vietnam is an attractive location for OEM electrical component assembly with a large low cost labour force, port access and located at the centre of ASEAN but with good proximity to China and Japan. Projected mine production capability for 2012 marks a significant change in the fairly low growth projections that have persisted for the past decade where expanding African and Chinese production has been offset by a declining contribution from North America and general stagnation in Latin America, Europe and Oceania. 

The projected 7.6% increase in year-on-year production capability for 2012 marks the start of a four-year growth period that should see global capability exceed 20Mt for the first time. The commissioning of both greenfield and brownfield expansion projects in Zambia and the DRC will result in a 55% surge in Africa from 2012 to 2015, a figure almost matched by a forecast 42% increase in Asia over the same period resulting largely from the continued ramp-up of Oyu Tolgoi to full production and an expected production spike at Grasberg. Only slightly less spectacular growth is expected from China (12%), North America (17%) and Latin America (also 17%, but equivalent to 1.3Mt of additional production), and with only Europe (9.3%), Middle East (8.7%) and Oceania (0.2%) forecast to increase production by less than 10% between 2012 and 2015. It should be noted that this projected growth comes from our “base case” scenario only and that while no additional production increases should be expected for 2012, a further 132kt could come from “highly probable” and “probable” projects in 2013

Disruptions since last quarter’s LTO have included some significant weather-related production losses at high-altitude mines in Chile which have been covered in more detail in our monthly updates. # Trends in consumption of secondary copper 

## Scrap definition 

Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap.  New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-based products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; and in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since th

ese could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. 

## Scrap consumption 

Copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) amounted to 8.39Mt in 2011, an increase of 4.8% on the prior year and accounting for 34.1% of copper consumed.  Direct use scrap took the lions share, representing some 57% of copper produced from scrap, with smelters (27%) and refineries (16%) producing copper from the balance. 

Growth in scrap use slowed in 2011 following the strong recovery in 2010, as a slowdown in the rate of price increase resulted slowed the relative increase in incentive to collect scrap while sluggish industrial production also limited scrap generation. # Principle uses of copper 

Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products.  Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use.  With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals.  This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and windi

ng wire. 

In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, construction is one of the largest sectors for consuming copper, accounting for 31% of total copper consumption.  The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. 

Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 

In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power distribution grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth, however, this is being offset by substitution to plastic tubing where this is possible.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for c

omfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 34% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors, connectors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers. In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried more quickly along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL). Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products. Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 9% of total copper consumption. The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military and civilian ordnance and coinage. The production of the Euro coin and the US presidential dollar coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products. However, copper’s use in coinage is now falling as national mints are beginning to respecify the composition of their coins to eliminate or reduce the copper content due to the rising cost of copper. With regard to the “price/market adjustment”, a negative adjustment implies that mine production needs to be lost (after allowing for highly-probable new projects, incremental expansions etc.) and vice-versa. A positive adjustment could be met either by new projects, incremental expansions or extensions to the mine-life of existing operations where closure is anticipated within the forecast period due to reserve depletions. These adjustments are made on an iterative basis, and are driven by the consumption forecast. These forecasts take into account the likely level of metal prices required to affect them, as well as the impact of changes in metal stocks on metal prices. Thus, during periods of surplus supplies, metal prices need to fall to a level sufficiently low to effect the closure of marginal mine capacity.
